1.title: Scheduling, Resources and Autoscaling
1.text: Welcome to Module six: Scheduling, Resources and Autoscaling. It covers the exam area Workloads and Scheduling. Each part of this module comes from the study notes of the same name, and every task was run on a real cluster, so you can read the notes after you watch.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do three things. Configure Pod admission and scheduling (limits, node affinity, and so on). Configure workload autoscaling. Practice with ten hands-on labs worth sixty-five points.

1.title: Where This Fits in the Exam
1.text: Here is where this module sits in the exam. Exam area: Workloads and Scheduling (fifteen percent). Practice in this module: ten labs, sixty-five points, about sixty-five minutes. Exam format: performance-based tasks in a live terminal, scored on the final cluster state. Validated on: Kubernetes version one point thirty-seven point zero.

1.title: How scheduling works
1.text: How scheduling works. The figure shows this: How the scheduler works. Exam tip: For a Pod stuck in Pending, run kube control describe pod and read the Failed Scheduling event.

1.title: How scheduling works, continued
1.text: How scheduling works. The scheduler takes each Pod without a node and picks one in two steps: filter (which nodes can run it: enough free resources, matching selectors, taints tolerated) and score (which of those is best). If the filter step leaves no node, the Pod stays Pending and kube control describe pod shows a Failed Scheduling event that says why (for example "Insufficient cpu", "node(s) didn't match Pod's node affinity or selector", "node(s) had untolerated taint"). That event is the first thing to read for any Pending Pod.

1.title: Requests, limits and QoS
1.text: Requests, limits and Qo S. resources dot requests. what the scheduler reserves for the container; used to choose a node. resources dot limits. the ceiling at run time; C P U over the limit is throttled, memory over the limit is O O M-killed. Exam tip: Requests decide where a Pod is scheduled; a container that uses more memory than its limit is O O M Killed.

1.title: Requests, limits and QoS, continued
1.text: Requests, limits and Qo S. The example is on the screen; read it line by line when you study.

1.title: Requests, limits and QoS, continued
1.text: Requests, limits and Qo S. kube control run has no the requests flag or the limits flag flags in the kube control used here (version one point thirty-six; kube control run the help flag lists only the env flag, the overrides flag, the port flag among the setting flags), so a Pod with resources is written in yamel (or created from the dry run flag set to client dash o yaml output). C P U is in cores ( one equals one core, one hundred millicores equals zero point one core). Memory is in bytes ( sixty-four mebibytes, one gibibyte ). A request larger than any node can offer (for example cpu one hundred ) keeps the Pod Pending forever (Lab six point eight). Qo S class (shown in dot status dot qos Class ) decides who is evicted first under memory pressure.

1.title: Requests, limits and QoS, continued
1.text: Requests, limits and Qo S. Guaranteed. every container has requests equals limits for C P U and memory. Burstable. at least one request or limit set, not Guaranteed. Best Effort. no requests or limits at all (evicted first).

1.title: Pod admission controls: LimitRange and ResourceQuota
1.text: Pod admission controls: Limit Range and Resource Quota. Both are checked when an object is created (admission), per namespace. Limit Range sets defaults and min or max per container or Pod. The example is on the screen; read it line by line when you study.

1.title: Pod admission controls: LimitRange and ResourceQuota, continued
1.text: Pod admission controls: Limit Range and Resource Quota. The defaults are written into the Pod at creation, so kube control get pod dash o yaml shows them. Existing Pods are not changed. Resource Quota caps the total for a namespace. The example is on the screen; read it line by line when you study.

1.title: Pod admission controls: LimitRange and ResourceQuota, continued
1.text: Pod admission controls: Limit Range and Resource Quota. If a quota covers C P U or memory, every new Pod must declare that resource (or a Limit Range must supply a default), otherwise it is rejected. A Deployment over quota does not fail loudly: the Replica Set cannot create the extra Pods. Read k dash n quota describe rs or k dash n quota get events for "exceeded quota" (Lab six point three).

1.title: Choosing nodes
1.text: Choosing nodes. node selector. simplest: Pod runs only on nodes with these labels. node name. bypass the scheduler (rarely used). Node affinity. richer rules: In, Not In, Exists; required or preferred. Pod affinity or anti-affinity. place Pods near or away from other Pods. Taints and tolerations. nodes repel Pods unless they tolerate. Topology spread constraints. spread Pods evenly across zones or nodes.

1.title: Choosing nodes, continued
1.text: Choosing nodes. The example is on the screen; read it line by line when you study.

1.title: Choosing nodes, continued
1.text: Choosing nodes. Node affinity (required). The example is on the screen; read it line by line when you study.

1.title: Choosing nodes, continued
1.text: Choosing nodes. required... is a hard rule: no match, Pod stays Pending. preferred... (with a weight ) is a soft rule. ...Ignored During Execution means Pods already running are not moved if labels change later. Pod anti-affinity (spread replicas across nodes). The example is on the screen; read it line by line when you study.

1.title: Choosing nodes, continued
1.text: Choosing nodes. Topology spread constraints ( topology Spread Constraints with max Skew, topology Key, when Unsatisfiable Do Not Schedule Schedule Anyway, label Selector ) spread replicas evenly. Trap found in the lab: the tainted control plane node still counts as an empty domain, so with Do Not Schedule only two of four replicas schedule on a two-worker cluster until you add node Taints Policy Honor (Lab six point one zero). With required and only N usable nodes, replica N plus one stays Pending. In the lab cluster the control plane is tainted, so two workers allow two replicas (Lab six point seven).

1.title: Taints and tolerations
1.text: Taints and tolerations. A taint on a node says "keep Pods away unless they tolerate me". Format key value effect. No Schedule. new Pods are not scheduled unless they tolerate it. Prefer No Schedule. the scheduler avoids the node if it can. No Execute. also evicts running Pods that do not tolerate it. Exam tip: A toleration allows a Pod onto a tainted node but does not attract it; remove a taint with key- at the end.

1.title: Taints and tolerations, continued
1.text: Taints and tolerations. The example is on the screen; read it line by line when you study.

1.title: Taints and tolerations, continued
1.text: Taints and tolerations. The example is on the screen; read it line by line when you study.

1.title: Taints and tolerations, continued
1.text: Taints and tolerations. A toleration only allows a Pod onto the node; it does not attract it. To force a Pod onto a tainted node, combine the toleration with a node selector or node affinity (Lab six point six). The control plane node carries the taint node role dot Kubernetes dot io slash control plane No Schedule, which is why Daemon Sets need the toleration to reach it.

1.title: Workload autoscaling
1.text: Workload autoscaling. The Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (H P A) changes a workload's replica count from observed metrics. The example is on the screen; read it line by line when you study. Exam tip: An H P A (Horizontal Pod Autoscaler) needs Metrics Server and C P U requests on the Pods.

1.title: Workload autoscaling, continued
1.text: Workload autoscaling. It needs the Metrics Server (the source for kube control top ) and the Pods must declare a C P U request: utilization is a percentage of the request. Without a request the H P A shows unknown and does not scale. Formula in words: desired replicas equals current replicas x (current utilization or target utilization), rounded up, kept between min and max. autoscaling slash version two also supports memory and custom metrics, and a behavior section for scale-up and scale-down speed. Vertical Pod Autoscaling (changing requests) is a separate add-on and is not part of the core exam objectives.

2.title: Lab 6.1: requests limits
2.text: Lab six point one: requests limits. This task is worth five points, and you should plan about five minutes. Start by switching to the kind-C K A context. In the namespace res, create a Pod sized (image engine X alpine ) with C P U request one hundred millicores, memory request sixty-four mebibytes, C P U limit two hundred millicores and memory limit one hundred twenty-eight mebibytes. Pause the video and try the task yourself, then come back for the solution.

2.title: Lab 6.1: requests limits, Solution
2.text: Here is one way to solve it. Run kube control dash n res run sized the image flag set to engine X alpine the dry run flag set to client dash o yaml slash tmp slash sized dot yaml. Then sed dash i s or ^ containers or containers or s or ^ resources or resources requests cpu one hundred millicores, memory sixty-four mebibytes, limits cpu two hundred millicores, memory one hundred twenty-eight mebibytes, and so on. Then kube control dash n res apply dash f slash tmp slash sized dot yaml. Then kube control dash n res wait the for flag set to condition Ready pod slash sized the timeout flag set to one hundred twenty seconds. Then kube control dash n res get pod sized dash o json path dot status dot qos Class. Then check the result with a read command, the way you would on the exam.

2.title: Lab 6.2: limitrange defaults
2.text: Lab six point two: limitrange defaults. This task is worth six points, and you should plan about six minutes. Start by switching to the kind-C K A context. In the namespace lr, create a Limit Range defaults so that containers without their own settings get a default C P U request of one hundred millicores, a default memory request of sixty-four mebibytes, a default C P U limit of two hundred fifty millicores and a default memory limit of one hundred twenty-eight mebibytes. Then create a Pod plain (image engine X alpine ) with no resource settings and show that it received the defaults. Pause the video and try the task yourself, then come back for the solution.

2.title: Lab 6.2: limitrange defaults, Solution
2.text: Here is one way to solve it. kube control dash n lr apply dash f -. The manifest comes next, as shown on the screen. Then kube control dash n lr run plain the image flag set to engine X alpine. Then kube control dash n lr wait the for flag set to condition Ready pod slash plain the timeout flag set to one hundred twenty seconds. Then kube control dash n lr get pod plain dash o json path dot spec dot containers zero dot resources. Then check the result with a read command, the way you would on the exam.

2.title: Lab 6.3: resourcequota
2.text: Lab six point three: resourcequota. This task is worth six points, and you should plan about six minutes. Start by switching to the kind-C K A context. In the namespace quota, create a Resource Quota team quota that allows at most three Pods, a total of one C P U in requests and one gibibyte of memory in requests. Then create a Deployment app with five replicas of engine X alpine whose containers request one hundred millicores C P U and sixty-four mebibytes memory each. Because of the quota, at most three Pods can run; find the reason in the events or the Replica Set. Pause the video and try the task yourself, then come back for the solution.

2.title: Lab 6.3: resourcequota, Solution
2.text: Here is one way to solve it. Run kube control dash n quota create quota team quota the hard flag set to pods three,requests dot cpu one,requests dot memory one gibibyte. Then kube control dash n quota create deployment app the image flag set to engine X alpine the replicas flag set to five. Then kube control dash n quota set resources deployment app the requests flag set to cpu one hundred millicores,memory sixty-four mebibytes. Then sleep ten. Then kube control dash n quota get pods. Then kube control dash n quota describe rs then pipe to grep dash i dash E exceeded then pipe to forbidden then pipe to head -three. Then kube control dash n quota describe quota team quota. Then check the result with a read command, the way you would on the exam.

2.title: Lab 6.4: nodeselector
2.text: Lab six point four: nodeselector. This task is worth five points, and you should plan about five minutes. Start by switching to the kind-C K A context. Label the node C K A worker two with disk ssd. In the namespace sched, create a Pod fast (image engine X alpine ) that can only run on nodes with this label, and check that it runs on C K A worker two. Pause the video and try the task yourself, then come back for the solution.

2.title: Lab 6.4: nodeselector, Solution
2.text: Here is one way to solve it. Run kube control label node C K A worker two disk ssd. kube control dash n sched apply dash f -. The manifest comes next, as shown on the screen. Then kube control dash n sched wait the for flag set to condition Ready pod slash fast the timeout flag set to one hundred twenty seconds. Then kube control dash n sched get pod fast dash o wide. Then check the result with a read command, the way you would on the exam.

2.title: Lab 6.5: node affinity
2.text: Lab six point five: node affinity. This task is worth seven points, and you should plan about seven minutes. Start by switching to the kind-C K A context. The node C K A worker carries the label tier gold. In the namespace aff, create a Deployment gold app with three replicas of engine X alpine that must be scheduled only on nodes whose label tier is gold. Use node affinity ( required During Scheduling Ignored During Execution ), not node selector. Pause the video and try the task yourself, then come back for the solution.

2.title: Lab 6.5: node affinity, Solution
2.text: Here is one way to solve it. kube control dash n aff apply dash f -. The manifest comes next, as shown on the screen. Then check the result with a read command, the way you would on the exam.

2.title: Lab 6.5: node affinity, Solution, continued
2.text: Lab six point five: node affinity, Solution, continued. Run - match Expressions. Then - key tier, operator In, values gold. Then containers. Then - name web, image engine X alpine. Then Y. Then kube control dash n aff rollout status deployment gold app the timeout flag set to one hundred twenty seconds. Then kube control dash n aff get pods dash o wide.

2.title: Lab 6.6: taint toleration
2.text: Lab six point six: taint toleration. This task is worth seven points, and you should plan about seven minutes. Start by switching to the kind-C K A context. Taint the node C K A worker two with dedicated db No Schedule. In the namespace taint, create a Pod db (image engine X alpine ) that tolerates this taint and is placed on C K A worker two using node selector on the label Kubernetes dot io slash hostname. Pause the video and try the task yourself, then come back for the solution.

2.title: Lab 6.6: taint toleration, Solution
2.text: Here is one way to solve it. Run kube control taint node C K A worker two dedicated db No Schedule. kube control dash n taint apply dash f -. The manifest comes next, as shown on the screen. Then kube control dash n taint wait the for flag set to condition Ready pod slash db the timeout flag set to one hundred twenty seconds. Then check the result with a read command, the way you would on the exam.

3.title: Lab 6.7: pod anti affinity
3.text: Lab six point seven: pod anti affinity. This task is worth seven points, and you should plan about seven minutes. Start by switching to the kind-C K A context. In the namespace spread, create a Deployment ha web with two replicas of engine X alpine. Make the scheduler guarantee that the two Pods never run on the same node, using required Pod anti-affinity on the node hostname ( Kubernetes dot io slash hostname ) for Pods with the label app ha web. Pause the video and try the task yourself, then come back for the solution.

3.title: Lab 6.7: pod anti affinity, Solution
3.text: Here is one way to solve it. kube control dash n spread apply dash f -. The manifest comes next, as shown on the screen. Then check the result with a read command, the way you would on the exam.

3.title: Lab 6.7: pod anti affinity, Solution, continued
3.text: Lab six point seven: pod anti affinity, Solution, continued. Run match Labels app ha web. Then topology Key Kubernetes dot io slash hostname. Then containers. Then - name web, image engine X alpine. Then Y. Then kube control dash n spread rollout status deployment ha web the timeout flag set to one hundred twenty seconds. Then kube control dash n spread get pods dash o wide.

3.title: Lab 6.8: fix pending pod
3.text: Lab six point eight: fix pending pod. This task is worth six points, and you should plan about six minutes. Start by switching to the kind-C K A context. In the namespace pend, the Pod big stays Pending. Find the reason with kube control describe and fix it so the Pod runs. Keep the Pod name big and the image engine X alpine; a C P U request above five hundred millicores is not acceptable. (A Pod's resources cannot be edited in place; recreate it.). Pause the video and try the task yourself, then come back for the solution.

3.title: Lab 6.8: fix pending pod, Solution
3.text: Here is one way to solve it. Run kube control dash n pend describe pod big then pipe to grep dash i -A two Failed Scheduling. Then kube control dash n pend delete pod big the force flag the grace period flag zero. kube control dash n pend apply dash f -. The manifest comes next, as shown on the screen. Then kube control dash n pend wait the for flag set to condition Ready pod slash big the timeout flag set to one hundred twenty seconds. Then check the result with a read command, the way you would on the exam.

3.title: Lab 6.9: hpa
3.text: Lab six point nine: hpa. This task is worth eight points, and you should plan about eight minutes. Start by switching to the kind-C K A context. In the namespace auto, the Deployment scaler ( engine X alpine, two replicas) exists without resource requests. Configure autoscaling for it: give the container a C P U request of one hundred millicores, and create a Horizontal Pod Autoscaler named scaler that keeps between two and six replicas and targets sixty percent average C P U utilization. The H P A must report its current C P U metric (not unknown ). Pause the video and try the task yourself, then come back for the solution.

3.title: Lab 6.9: hpa, Solution
3.text: Here is one way to solve it. Run kube control dash n auto set resources deployment scaler the requests flag set to cpu one hundred millicores. Then kube control dash n auto rollout status deployment scaler the timeout flag set to one hundred twenty seconds. Then kube control dash n auto autoscale deployment scaler the min flag set to two the max flag set to six the cpu flag set to sixty percent. Then for i in seq one thirty do dash n kube control dash n auto get hpa scaler dash o json path dot status dot current Metrics zero dot resource dot current dot average Utilization, and so on. Then kube control dash n auto get hpa scaler. Then check the result with a read command, the way you would on the exam.

3.title: Lab 6.10: topology spread
3.text: Lab six point one zero: topology spread. This task is worth eight points, and you should plan about eight minutes. Start by switching to the kind-C K A context. In the namespace tsc, create a Deployment even with four replicas of engine X alpine (label app even ) that must be spread evenly across the nodes: use a topology spread constraint on the node hostname ( Kubernetes dot io slash hostname ) with max Skew one, and do not schedule a Pod if the constraint cannot be met ( Do Not Schedule ). The control plane node is tainted and cannot run these Pods, so it must not count as an empty domain: set node Taints Policy Honor. Both worker nodes must end up with two Pods each. Pause the video and try the task yourself, then come back for the solution.

3.title: Lab 6.10: topology spread, Solution
3.text: Here is one way to solve it. kube control dash n tsc apply dash f -. The manifest comes next, as shown on the screen. Then check the result with a read command, the way you would on the exam.

3.title: Lab 6.10: topology spread, Solution, continued
3.text: Lab six point one zero: topology spread, Solution, continued. Run node Taints Policy Honor. Then label Selector match Labels app even. Then containers. Then - name web, image engine X alpine. Then Y. Then kube control dash n tsc rollout status deployment even the timeout flag set to one hundred twenty seconds. Then kube control dash n tsc get pods dash o wide.

3.title: Recall Check 1
3.text: Recall check one. Say each answer out loud before you listen to mine. Question one. A Pod is Pending. Where is the reason? Answer: The Failed Scheduling event in kube control describe pod. Question two. What happens to a container that exceeds its memory limit? Its C P U limit? Answer: Memory: O O M-killed. C P U: throttled. Question three. Which Qo S class has requests equal to limits for every container? Answer: Guaranteed.

3.title: Recall Check 2
3.text: Recall check two. Say each answer out loud before you listen to mine. Question four. What is the difference between a Limit Range and a Resource Quota? Answer: Limit Range sets defaults and bounds per container or Pod; Resource Quota caps the namespace total. Question five. A Deployment in a namespace with a Pod-count quota stops at three Pods. Where do you see why? Answer: In the events of the Replica Set ( describe rs ) or kube control get events. Question six. Does a toleration make a Pod run on the tainted node? Answer: No; it only allows it. Add a node selector or affinity to attract it.

3.title: Recall Check 3
3.text: Recall check three. Say each answer out loud before you listen to mine. Question seven. Which taint effect evicts running Pods? Answer: No Execute. Question eight. What two things does an H P A on C P U need? Answer: The Metrics Server and a C P U request on the Pods.

3.title: Module Recap
3.text: Here is the recap. Pending Pod: describe pod, read Failed Scheduling. Resources: requests schedule, limits cap; memory over limit equals O O M Killed. Qo S: Guaranteed, Burstable, Best Effort. Admission: Limit Range (defaults or bounds), Resource Quota (namespace total). Placement: node selector, node affinity, pod (anti-)affinity, topology spread. Taint: kube control taint node n key value effect; remove with key-. Toleration: allows, does not attract. H P A: kube control autoscale... the min flag the max flag the cpu flag set to fifty percent; needs Metrics Server and C P U requests. In the next module, we continue the course.
